list.item: The thickness \(t\) in millimeters of a folded sheet of paper after it is folded \(n\) times is given by the equation \(t=(0.05) \cdot 2^n\).

div.para: The sheet of paper is 0.05 mm thick.

list.item: What does the number 0.05 represent in the equation?

div.para: The number 2 indicates that the thickness doubles with each increment of \(n\), the number of folds.

list.item: What does the number 2 represent in the equation?

solution.para: Here is a table of values for the thickness of the paper after different numbers of folds:

image.alt: 7 points on coordinate plane, showing exponential growth. Horizontal axis from 0 to 8, labeled number of folds. Vertical axis from 0 to 4, labeled thickness in millimeters.

div.para: It takes 5 folds before the paper is more than 1 mm thick. After 4 folds, the paper is 0.8 mm thick, and after 5 folds, it is 1.6 mm thick. It takes 8 folds before the paper is more than 1 cm or 10 mm thick (1.28 cm to be precise).

The \(y\)-intercept represents the initial thickness of the paper \(t\) before folding (when \(n\) is zero). Calculate the value of the \(y\)-intercept.

div.para: In this equation, the value of thickness of the paper \(t\) becomes larger as the number of folds \(n\) increases (approaches infinity). This means that, as the paper is folded an increasing number of times, the thickness has the potential to be infinite, but in reality, it can never quite reach it.
